title: The Indus Valley Civilisation
description: South Asia's first urban culture — and its undeciphered script

concepts.title: Cities Without Kings
concepts.contentHtml:
The Indus Valley Civilisation (also called Harappan) flourished from roughly 3300 to 1300 BCE across what is now Pakistan and north-western India. At its height around 2500 BCE it was the largest of the world's three contemporary great civilisations — alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia — covering an area larger than either.

Its two best-known cities, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, were home to perhaps 30,000–40,000 people each. They featured a level of urban planning unmatched in their era: grid-pattern streets, standardised baked-brick construction, sophisticated drainage and sewage systems, and the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro — a watertight tank possibly used for ritual bathing.

Curiously, no monumental palaces, royal tombs, or unambiguous depictions of rulers have been found. The Harappans appear to have been remarkably egalitarian by ancient standards — or simply organised differently from the kings-and-temples model that defines Egypt and Mesopotamia.

concepts.title: Trade, Weights, and the Mystery Script
concepts.contentHtml:
The Harappans operated one of the world's first long-distance trade networks. Their seals, made of carved steatite, have been found as far afield as Mesopotamian Ur — recording goods such as cotton, beads, copper, and timber moving along the Indus, by sea down the Persian Gulf, and overland to Central Asia.

Standardised weights and measures across all cities — even those a thousand kilometres apart — suggest centralised regulation of commerce. The unit system was binary in small weights and decimal in larger ones, a hybrid not seen elsewhere.

The Indus script, found on thousands of seals, remains one of archaeology's most stubborn mysteries. With around 400 distinct signs and inscriptions averaging only five symbols long, no Rosetta-Stone-style bilingual text has ever been found. Whether the script encodes a full language at all is still debated. It is one of the oldest writing systems still undeciphered.

concepts.title: Decline and the Vedic Period
concepts.contentHtml:
By 1900 BCE the great cities were already shrinking, and by 1300 BCE most were abandoned. The reasons remain debated: shifts in the course of the Sarasvati and Indus rivers, prolonged drought caused by weakening monsoons, soil salinisation from over-irrigation, and possibly disease all contributed. There is no evidence of violent invasion.

What followed in the second millennium BCE was the gradual arrival of Indo-Aryan peoples speaking an early form of Sanskrit. They composed the Vedas — the oldest religious texts of Hinduism — beginning around 1500 BCE. The Vedic period saw the formation of the early caste system, sacred Sanskrit literature, and the Mahajanapadas: sixteen great kingdoms whose competition would shape classical India.

The relationship between Indus Valley and Vedic culture is hotly contested. Some elements of later Hinduism — sacred bathing, fertility figurines, certain animal symbols — may have Harappan roots, suggesting cultural continuity rather than a clean break.

title: The Maurya and Gupta Empires
description: Classical India — Ashoka, the spread of Buddhism, and the golden age of mathematics

concepts.title: The Maurya Empire and Ashoka
concepts.contentHtml:
In 322 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya seized the throne of Magadha and quickly built South Asia's first unified subcontinental empire. By the reign of his grandson Ashoka the Great (268–232 BCE), the Maurya Empire stretched from modern Afghanistan to eastern Bengal and well into the Deccan — over 5 million square kilometres.

Ashoka's transformation is one of history's most remarkable. After the brutal conquest of Kalinga (modern Odisha) in 261 BCE — which according to his own account left 100,000 dead and 150,000 deported — he renounced military expansion and converted to Buddhism. He inscribed his ethical edicts onto rock pillars across the empire (the Ashokan Edicts, written in Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts), establishing dhamma — moral law — as state policy.

He sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka, the Hellenistic world, and Southeast Asia. Within centuries, Buddhism reached China, Korea, and Japan. Ashoka's wheel — the Ashoka Chakra — sits today at the centre of India's national flag.

concepts.title: The Gupta Golden Age
concepts.contentHtml:
After several centuries of fragmentation, the Gupta Empire (c. 320–550 CE) reunified northern India and presided over a period commonly called India's classical golden age.

Gupta achievements were extraordinary:

  • Mathematics: Aryabhata (476–550 CE) worked with the place-value decimal system (Brahmagupta, in 628, later set out rules for zero as a number), calculated π to four decimal places, and proposed that Earth rotates on its axis.
  • Astronomy: predicted eclipses with high accuracy.
  • Medicine: the Sushruta Samhita and Charaka Samhita codified surgery, including rhinoplasty.
  • Literature: Kalidasa, often called the Indian Shakespeare, wrote in Sanskrit.
  • Art: the cave paintings at Ajanta and the Hindu temples of the period set the templates for South Asian art for a millennium.

The decimal numerals, including the symbol for zero, eventually reached Europe via Arab mathematicians — which is why we still call them 'Arabic numerals' even though the system originated in Gupta India.

concepts.title: Religion and Society
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical period reshaped Indian religion. Buddhism spread widely under royal patronage but began to decline within India by the late Gupta period, surviving more strongly abroad. Jainism, founded by Mahavira in the 6th century BCE, persisted as a smaller but influential tradition emphasising non-violence (ahimsa).

Hinduism itself underwent major transformation. The Bhakti movement, emphasising personal devotion to deities like Vishnu and Shiva, displaced the older Vedic ritual sacrifice. The Bhagavad Gita, part of the larger Mahabharata epic, was composed during this period and remains one of Hinduism's central texts.

Society was structured around the four-fold varna system — Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (warriors), Vaishyas (merchants), Shudras (labourers) — with castes (jatis) emerging as a finer-grained classification underlying everyday life. The Gupta era is often viewed as the consolidation of classical Hindu society's enduring patterns.

title: Medieval South Asia
description: Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, and the meeting of Hindu and Islamic worlds

concepts.title: The Delhi Sultanate
concepts.contentHtml:
Islam first reached the subcontinent through Arab traders along the Malabar Coast in the 7th century, but military penetration came centuries later. After the Ghurid invasions of the 12th century, Qutb-ud-din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 — beginning over 300 years of Turko-Afghan Muslim rule over much of north India.

The Sultanate passed through five dynasties: the Mamluks, Khaljis, Tughluqs, Sayyids, and Lodis. Its reach varied — at its peak under Muhammad bin Tughluq (1325–51), it briefly controlled almost the entire subcontinent — but administrative cohesion was fragile.

The Sultanate left a permanent architectural mark, including Delhi's Qutb Minar (1199, the world's tallest brick minaret at 73 m) and the broader Indo-Islamic synthesis that fused Persian arches and domes with Indian carving traditions. It also brought Persian as a court and literary language and saw the emergence of Urdu through the daily mixing of Persian, Arabic, and local Indo-Aryan languages.

concepts.title: Vijayanagara and the South
concepts.contentHtml:
While Muslim sultans ruled the north, southern India was dominated by the Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646). Founded by the brothers Harihara and Bukka, it rose specifically as a Hindu bulwark against Islamic expansion southward and became one of the wealthiest states in the medieval world.

Its capital, also called Vijayanagara (modern Hampi), was — by the early 16th century — among the largest cities on Earth, with perhaps 500,000 people. Portuguese travellers compared it to Rome. Its temples, royal precincts, elephant stables, and aqueducts still cover 25 km² of UNESCO-protected ruins.

Vijayanagara's economy depended on cotton textiles, spices, and the diamond mines of Golconda. Its rulers patronised Telugu, Kannada, and Tamil literature, sustaining a flourishing southern Hindu culture even as the north grew more deeply Islamicised. The empire fell after a coalition of Deccan sultanates crushed it at the Battle of Talikota in 1565.

concepts.title: Bhakti, Sufism, and Cultural Synthesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Medieval South Asia was not a simple confrontation of two faiths. Two parallel devotional movements profoundly shaped popular religion:

  • The Bhakti movement stressed direct personal devotion to a deity — Krishna, Rama, or Shiva — rather than priestly mediation. Saints like Kabir, Mirabai, Tulsidas, and Surdas wrote in regional languages, undermining Brahminical Sanskrit monopoly and challenging caste.
  • Sufism, the mystical strand of Islam, emphasised an inward path to God through love, music, and the guidance of saints (pirs). The shrines of figures like Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer) and Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi) attracted Hindu and Muslim pilgrims alike — and still do.

From their interaction came new syntheses. Guru Nanak (1469–1539), drawing on both traditions, founded Sikhism, declaring 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim — only one God.' Hindustani classical music, qawwali, Urdu poetry, and Indo-Islamic cuisine all emerged from this remarkably productive cultural overlap.

title: The Mughal Empire
description: Akbar, Shah Jahan, and the Taj — power, art, and decline

concepts.title: Foundation and Akbar's Synthesis
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1526, the Central Asian prince Babur — a descendant of both Tamerlane and Genghis Khan — defeated the Lodi Sultan at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. Within a few decades it would govern most of the subcontinent.

The empire's defining ruler was Babur's grandson Akbar the Great (1556–1605), who took power at age 13 and steadily extended Mughal control from Kabul to Bengal. Akbar's distinctive contribution was political and religious accommodation in a multi-confessional empire:

  • Abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims.
  • Married Hindu Rajput princesses, integrating their families into Mughal nobility.
  • Founded the syncretic Din-i-Ilahi philosophy drawing on Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, and Christianity.
  • Created the mansabdar ranked-officer system for administration.
  • Held theological debates among scholars of every major religion at his court at Fatehpur Sikri.

Population estimates put Akbar's empire at roughly 100 million people, perhaps a fifth of humanity at the time.

concepts.title: Apogee and the Taj Mahal
concepts.contentHtml:
Under Akbar's son Jahangir and grandson Shah Jahan (1628–58), the empire reached its cultural apex. Mughal painting, miniature illumination, and architecture combined Persian and Indian aesthetics into a distinct, refined style.

Shah Jahan's most famous monument is the Taj Mahal in Agra (built 1632–53), a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal who died in childbirth. Its perfectly symmetrical white-marble dome, set above reflective gardens divided into the four quarters of paradise, is universally considered the masterpiece of Mughal architecture and one of the most recognisable buildings on Earth. Around 20,000 craftsmen worked on it for more than two decades.

The empire's economic might was equally impressive. By the early 1700s, Mughal India produced about a quarter of global GDP — roughly tied with Qing China — driven by cotton textiles exported across the Indian Ocean and into Europe. India was the world's manufacturing centre well before the Industrial Revolution shifted that role to Britain.

concepts.title: Aurangzeb and the Long Decline
concepts.contentHtml:
The reign of Shah Jahan's son Aurangzeb (1658–1707) marked the empire's last expansion — and its overextension. Aurangzeb pursued conquest into the Deccan with relentless campaigns lasting decades. He reimposed the jizya, demolished some Hindu temples, and reversed Akbar's policy of accommodation.

By his death the empire was nominally larger than ever — but its treasury was depleted, the Marathas under Shivaji had built a powerful Hindu confederacy, the Sikhs were militarising under their Gurus, and provincial governors were turning increasingly autonomous.

Eighteenth-century Mughal authority unravelled rapidly. Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739, carrying off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. Maratha armies dominated the Deccan and central India by 1750. The British East India Company won the Battle of Plassey in 1757 — the first decisive step in a colonial takeover that would soon eclipse the Mughals entirely. The last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, would be exiled to Burma after the failed 1857 uprising.

title: Colonial Era to Independence
description: British Raj, Gandhi, Partition, and the modern subcontinent

concepts.title: Company Rule and the Raj
concepts.contentHtml:
The British East India Company began as a trading enterprise in 1600 but gradually became a territorial power. Its victory at Plassey in 1757 — engineered as much by bribery of Bengali nobles as by combat — gave it Bengal, the richest province of Mughal India. By 1818 the Company controlled most of the subcontinent through a mix of direct rule and subordinate princely states.

The 1857 Indian Rebellion (also called the Sepoy Mutiny or India's First War of Independence) shook the system to its core. After brutal suppression, Britain abolished Company rule and brought India under direct Crown rule — the British Raj (1858–1947). Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876.

The economic effects were enormous and contested. The Raj built railways (40,000 km by 1900), the postal and telegraph systems, and English-medium education — but Indian textile production was dismantled in favour of British imports, multiple severe famines (1876–78, 1899–1900, 1943) killed tens of millions, and India's share of world manufacturing fell from ~25 % in 1750 to ~2 % by 1900.

concepts.title: The Independence Movement
concepts.contentHtml:
The Indian National Congress formed in 1885, initially as a moderate forum for Indian professionals to petition the Raj. By the early 20th century it had become the principal vehicle for self-government and, eventually, independence.

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948), trained as a barrister in London and politically radicalised in South Africa, returned to India in 1915 and transformed the movement. His tactic of satyagraha — non-violent resistance — produced epoch-making campaigns:

  • The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22).
  • The Salt March (1930) — a 390 km walk to make salt from the sea in defiance of the British monopoly.
  • The Quit India Movement (1942) demanding immediate British withdrawal.

Alongside Gandhi worked Jawaharlal Nehru (Congress's heir apparent), Subhas Chandra Bose (who allied with Japan during World War II), and Bhimrao Ambedkar (champion of Dalit rights and chief author of the eventual Indian constitution). The Muslim League under Muhammad Ali Jinnah increasingly advocated a separate Muslim state.

concepts.title: Partition and the Modern Subcontinent
concepts.contentHtml:
British India was partitioned into two independent states on 14–15 August 1947: the Hindu-majority India and the Muslim-majority Pakistan (initially in two wings, East and West). The boundaries — drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in barely six weeks — split Punjab and Bengal.

The result was the largest forced migration in human history: roughly 15 million people crossed borders, and estimates of the dead in communal violence range from about 200,000 to 2 million. Millions of women were abducted. Refugee trains arrived bearing only corpses. The trauma scars relations between India and Pakistan to this day.

Subsequent decades produced:

  • India-Pakistan wars in 1947, 1965 and 1971 (and the 1999 Kargil conflict) and ongoing tensions over Kashmir.
  • The 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War, in which East Pakistan broke away to become Bangladesh after a brutal civil war and Indian military intervention.
  • India's emergence as the world's largest democracy and, since 2023, its most populous country.
  • Both India and Pakistan acquiring nuclear weapons (1974/1998 and 1998 respectively).
  • Sustained economic transformation in India after 1991 liberalisation, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty.

South Asia today is home to roughly a quarter of humanity — and remains one of the most strategically and culturally consequential regions on Earth.
